items.prompt: As this unit defines it, what does a sponsor do that a mentor doesn't?
choices: Uses their own influence and credibility to advocate for you in rooms you're not in
Gives you private advice whenever you ask for it
Formally manages your performance review
Introduces you to people at other companies
items.explanation: A mentor's support stays inside the conversation you had with them. A sponsor actively vouches for you elsewhere, using their own standing, specifically when you have no voice in the room.
items.reference:
🗣️ Mentor = advice, privately, when asked
🛡️ Sponsor = advocacy, in rooms you're not in

Why: Marcel speaking up for Priya in a leadership sync she wasn't part of is the worked example of sponsorship, not mentorship.

items.prompt: A colleague tells you privately, 'here's exactly what I'd say to your manager if I were you.' Is that colleague acting as your sponsor?
choices: No — that's mentorship, since the advice never leaves your private conversation
Yes, because the advice is specific and actionable
Yes, as long as you actually follow the advice
It depends only on how senior the colleague is
items.explanation: Sponsorship is defined by where the support happens, not by how good the advice is. Advice you could use yourself, however sharp, isn't the same as someone else making your case where you have no voice.
items.reference:
🗣️ Mentor = advice, privately, when asked
🛡️ Sponsor = advocacy, in rooms you're not in

Why: Marcel speaking up for Priya in a leadership sync she wasn't part of is the worked example of sponsorship, not mentorship.

items.prompt: What does a sponsor risk that a mentor generally doesn't, by advocating for you?
choices: Some of their own credibility and standing, since they're putting part of their reputation behind yours
Nothing real — advocacy is essentially free for the sponsor
Only their time, the same as a mentor
Their formal job title
items.explanation: Advocacy costs a sponsor something real: if they're wrong about you, or if it's remembered badly, that's on their own credibility. That's exactly why sponsorship has to be earned rather than requested.
items.reference:
🗣️ Mentor = advice, privately, when asked
🛡️ Sponsor = advocacy, in rooms you're not in

Why: Marcel speaking up for Priya in a leadership sync she wasn't part of is the worked example of sponsorship, not mentorship.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, why does Priya end up protected when the new director's reorg hits, while Marcus doesn't?
choices: Priya spent two years being genuinely useful to a senior engineer who's now willing to advocate for her; Marcus has friendly colleagues but no one who has ever actually vouched for him
Priya is more senior than Marcus
Priya's manager personally intervened
Marcus never noticed the reorg was happening
items.explanation: Both engineers face the identical unfair situation. The difference is entirely that Priya had built a real sponsor relationship over time, and Marcus, despite having plenty of friendly colleagues, had no one whose advocacy carried real weight.

items.prompt: What specifically does the senior engineer do in L1's scenario that makes it sponsorship rather than mentorship?
choices: He brings it up with the director himself, unprompted, in a meeting Priya isn't in
He tells Priya privately what she should say to the director
He forwards Priya some advice articles about handling reorgs
He agrees with Priya over lunch that the reorg seems unfair
items.explanation: The defining moment is that the advocacy happens in a room Priya isn't part of, using his own standing to say it — exactly the gap a mentor's private advice can't close.

items.prompt: How does this unit's 'coalition-building as defense' relate to the broader idea covered in the white unit?
choices: White covers legitimate influence-building generally; this unit is a specific application of it aimed at building protection before you need it
They describe unrelated, competing strategies
This unit replaces white's model entirely with a defensive-only framework
White is only about influence with peers, while this unit is only about influence with managers
items.explanation: White establishes legitimate influence in general (reciprocity, being visibly useful). Coalition-building as defense narrows that to one specific purpose: building alliances in advance of needing protection.
items.reference: Why: This unit doesn't introduce a new theory of influence — it applies white's general model to one specific, defensive purpose.

items.prompt: What mistake does this unit say most people make about mentors and sponsors?
choices: Assuming that having a mentor provides the same protection a sponsor would, when it doesn't
Assuming sponsors are more common than mentors
Assuming mentors are always more senior than sponsors
Assuming you can only have one or the other, never both
items.explanation: Most people do have mentors, and mistakenly believe that's equivalent protection to having a sponsor. It isn't — a mentor's support never has to leave the private conversation it happened in.

items.prompt: According to this unit, why can't a sponsor relationship be built quickly, in a crisis?
choices: Because real trust and a real track record take sustained time to build, and can't be manufactured urgently
Because sponsors are legally required to wait a fixed period before advocating for anyone
Because most senior people are too busy to ever become sponsors
Because crises make people more willing to advocate for others, not less
items.explanation: The unit is explicit: sponsorship requires a sustained pattern of being useful, which by definition takes time. Trying to compress that under pressure doesn't produce the same result.

items.prompt: Why does waiting until you're already under attack to start building alliances tend to fail?
choices: Because the trust a real alliance requires takes a track record to build, and there's no time left to build one once trouble has already started
Because people under attack are legally barred from asking for help
Because alliances built during a crisis are always noticed and reported
Because it's technically impossible to talk to senior people during a difficult period
items.explanation: The core problem isn't etiquette — it's that real trust takes time to accumulate, and a crisis doesn't grant you that time retroactively.

items.prompt: What is 'the honesty line' as this unit defines it?
choices: The difference between genuinely being useful and trustworthy versus performing friendliness purely as self-protection
A rule about never discussing salary with a potential sponsor
A requirement to disclose to someone that you consider them a potential sponsor
The point at which a mentor becomes a sponsor automatically
items.explanation: The honesty line separates real usefulness (which would exist even without a defensive purpose) from transactional flattery aimed only at self-protection.

items.prompt: Why does a coalition built purely on transactional flattery tend to be fragile?
choices: Because it was never built on anything real, so it tends to collapse exactly when it's tested
Because flattery is illegal in most workplaces
Because flattery always gets discovered within a week
Because transactional relationships are actually stronger, just shorter-lived
items.explanation: A relationship with no substance underneath the performance has nothing to draw on when it's actually tested — which tends to be the exact moment real backing would matter most.

items.prompt: What does this unit mean by 'the trust-and-track-record timeline'?
choices: The fact that sponsorship is earned through a sustained pattern over time, not a single favor or a well-timed compliment
A formal HR process for requesting a sponsor
The average number of years before any two colleagues become friends
A schedule for when to ask a sponsor for a promotion
items.explanation: It names the honest reality that sponsorship isn't granted in a moment — it accumulates from a sustained, real pattern, which directly connects to favor-economy's idea of banking goodwill before you need to spend it.

items.prompt: In L1's facts panel, what marks the moment the mentor/sponsor difference actually shows up?
choices: The moment you're not in the room
The moment you ask for advice
The moment a performance review happens
The moment you change teams
items.explanation: The facts panel is explicit: the difference between a mentor and a sponsor only becomes visible when you're not present to advocate for yourself.

Bad decisions you might make on your own
Being asked to work extra hours
Getting negative feedback from a peer
items.explanation: A mentor helps you make better decisions yourself. A sponsor's advocacy specifically covers the case where a decision is being made about you and you're not there to speak for yourself.

A formal fee paid to HR
Nothing extra — the cost is identical for both roles
Their entire relationship with the person they're advocating to
items.explanation: A mentor's cost is their time. A sponsor's cost is real: their own credibility is on the line if the advocacy turns out to be misplaced.

items.prompt: A colleague explains, in a private conversation, exactly what they would say to your manager on your behalf if they were you. Per L2, does this alone make them your sponsor?
choices: No — sponsorship is about where the support happens, not how useful the advice is; this is still mentorship until it's said in a room without you
Yes, since the content of the advice matches what a sponsor would say
Yes, as long as they say it with confidence
It depends on their job title
items.explanation: The distinguishing factor is always location: does the support happen in your presence (mentorship) or when you're absent, backed by their own standing (sponsorship)?

items.prompt: Per L2's timeline, what characterizes the earliest phase (months 1-6) of building a real sponsor relationship?
choices: Consistently useful in small, low-stakes ways, without it being noticed as 'relationship-building'
A single, large, visible gesture aimed at getting noticed quickly
Explicitly asking the senior person to be your sponsor
Frequent, scheduled 1:1s specifically about career strategy
items.explanation: The timeline is explicit that the earliest phase is just doing good work repeatedly and quietly, not a deliberate campaign to be seen — which is exactly what makes it durable later.

items.prompt: Per L2's timeline, what shifts around months 18+ in a real sponsor relationship?
choices: Enough of a track record exists that the senior person would advocate for you without being asked
The relationship becomes formalized through an HR program
The senior person starts asking you for favors in return
The relationship typically ends, since 18 months is the natural limit
items.explanation: By that point, the accumulated evidence is enough that advocacy becomes a safe bet in the senior person's own judgment — not something that has to be requested.

items.prompt: How does L2 connect this unit's timeline to favor-economy?
choices: A sponsor relationship is framed as the largest, highest-trust kind of goodwill withdrawal, needing the deepest deposit history behind it
Favor-economy and this unit describe entirely separate, unrelated processes
Favor-economy is presented as a faster shortcut that replaces the need for a sponsor
This unit argues favor-economy's model doesn't apply to sponsorship at all
items.explanation: L2 explicitly borrows favor-economy's deposit/withdrawal framing: sponsorship, being the highest-trust ask there is, requires the deepest history of genuine deposits.

items.prompt: Per L2, what happens when someone tries to compress the sponsor-building timeline under pressure — for example, right before a layoff?
choices: The sudden, need-timed attentiveness tends to look like exactly what it is, and an experienced senior person is likely to notice the timing
It usually works just as well, since senior people rarely notice timing
It's technically impossible to attempt, so the question doesn't arise
It always backfires by making the senior person actively hostile
items.explanation: L2 is direct about this: sudden, urgent attentiveness aimed at someone with influence, timed to exactly when you need help, reads as exactly what it is rather than as a track record.

items.prompt: Per L2, why is a senior person especially likely to notice a compressed, need-timed attempt at coalition-building?
choices: Because the person with real standing to protect is also the one most likely to recognize the timing as self-interested rather than genuine
Because most senior people keep detailed logs of everyone's behavior
Because compressed attempts are always announced explicitly
Because junior employees are legally required to disclose their intentions
items.explanation: The unit ties this to the sponsor's own incentives: someone with real standing to protect has good reason to scrutinize sudden, conveniently-timed attentiveness before extending their own credibility.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does the honesty distinction matter practically, not just ethically?
choices: A manipulated relationship is fragile exactly when it's tested, which tends to be the moment real backing would matter most
It matters only for legal compliance reasons
It has no practical effect — the outcome is the same either way
Genuine relationships are always faster to build than manipulative ones
items.explanation: L2 makes the practical case directly: a relationship built on performance rather than substance collapses under scrutiny, and scrutiny tends to arrive at the exact moment sponsorship would be needed most.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's the defining test that separates genuine coalition-building from transactional manipulation?
choices: Whether the relationship and the useful work would exist even if you never ended up needing defending
Whether the senior person is aware the relationship is happening
Whether you eventually ask the person to be your sponsor directly
Whether the relationship is documented in writing
items.explanation: L2's test is whether the underlying usefulness is real and independent of the outcome — genuine coalition-building would have happened anyway, even with no defensive payoff.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's missing from a transactional, manipulation-based attempt at coalition-building that a genuine one has?
choices: Any real substance underneath the performance of friendliness
A clear job title for the senior person
A written record of every interaction
Regular scheduled meetings
items.explanation: L2 describes the transactional version as performance with nothing real underneath it — which is exactly why it doesn't hold up when actually tested.

items.prompt: Per L2's worked contrast, what does a mentor actually do in the specific moment a decision is being made about you, in a room you're not in?
choices: Nothing directly — a mentor's help is confined to conversations you're actually part of
They step into the room and advocate on your behalf
They automatically get notified and can weigh in remotely
They take over chairing the meeting
items.explanation: L2's contrast is precise: a mentor's value doesn't extend into rooms they're not part of. That gap is exactly what a sponsor's advocacy fills.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's the most a mentor can do to help with a decision being made about you that they're not part of?
choices: Help you prepare beforehand or debrief afterward, but not affect what's said while it's happening
Silently attend the meeting without speaking
Delegate their advocacy to someone else
Formally request to be added to the meeting
items.explanation: A mentor's usefulness is real but bounded by presence — they can prepare you before or help you process after, but they can't be the voice in the room itself the way a sponsor can.

Whether Marcel would ever find out about the decision

items.prompt: Per L3, why does Marcel's advocacy actually work in the leadership sync?

items.explanation: L3 is explicit that it works specifically because Marcel's credibility is real and independently earned, and the advocacy is unprompted — not because Priya requested it or because of Marcel's rank alone.

items.prompt: Per L3's extension discussion, what should someone new to an organization, without years to build a sponsor relationship yet, actually do?

items.explanation: L3 is honest that you can't manufacture years of trust on demand — the answer is to begin the real timeline immediately and use a mentor plus documented track record as a partial, not equivalent, substitute in the meantime.

items.prompt: Why does L3 say a documented track record only partially substitutes for a sponsor when you're new to an organization?

Because documentation takes longer to build than a sponsor relationship does
items.explanation: L3 draws a clear line: documentation strengthens your own case, but it can't stand in a room and speak on your behalf the way a sponsor's advocacy does — it lowers the need without closing the gap.

items.prompt: Per L3's extension discussion, does building a sponsor relationship require personal warmth with that person?

items.explanation: L3 explicitly separates the two: the usefulness has to be genuine, but it doesn't have to be friendly to be genuine — a sponsor relationship can be built purely on a credible, direct track record of good work.

items.prompt: What would have made Priya's retry-logic conversation cross the honesty line, per L3?
